questions.incorrectFeedback: Scale the balance point, then shift it: E[3X − 2] = 3E[X] − 2 = 12 − 2 = 10.

questions.stem: For any X that has a mean and E[X²], which is always true?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — the gap E[X²] − (E[X])² is an average of squared distances from the mean, so it can't be negative.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X²] − (E[X])² is the average squared distance from the mean, never negative. So E[X²] ≥ (E[X])². (And the mean of a die, 3.5, is not a possible roll.)

questions.stem: X is the score on one roll of a fair die. E[X] is…
questions.correctFeedback: Right — (1 + 2 + … + 6)/6 = 3.5. The mean need not be a value X can take.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X] = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)/6 = 3.5. It's a balance point, not a face; nothing is rounded.

questions.stem: From Lesson 5: X is uniform on (0, 1/5). What is its density there?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct — height × width must be 1, and the width is 1/5, so the height is 5.
questions.incorrectFeedback: The area under the density must be 1. Width 1/5 forces height 5. Densities may exceed 1; only areas are probabilities.

questions.stem: X has density 2x on (0, 1). Where does it balance?
questions.correctFeedback: Yes — ∫ x · 2x dx from 0 to 1 = 2/3. More sand near 1 pulls the balance right of 1/2.
questions.incorrectFeedback: E[X] = ∫₀¹ x · 2x dx = [2x³/3]₀¹ = 2/3. The sand piles up toward 1, so the balance sits right of the midpoint, but not at the peak.
